title: Jamestown Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Jamestown wells have a 300 ft median depth, 6 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $25,500-$42,000.
h1: Jamestown, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Jamestown means understanding mountain-bedrock wells before you commit. Records within 5 miles show 2,204 permitted wells, with a median reported depth of 300 feet and a median reported pump yield of 6.0 gallons per minute.

These figures are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee what a new well will produce on a particular lot. Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, so nearby well records, geology, access, and the proposed building site all matter.

sections.heading: How deep are wells around Jamestown?
sections.html:
Jamestown wells are commonly drilled into fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. The median reported depth is 300 feet, while the middle half runs from 160 to 480 feet. That range is the practical starting point for discussing a drilling bid, not a promise about your parcel.

Depth varies substantially. Thirteen percent of recorded wells are under 100 feet, 35% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 37% fall from 300 to 600 feet. Another 15% reach 600 feet or more. The 90th-percentile depth is 620 feet, and the deepest record is 1,428 feet. Nearby Bark Ranch, Lazy Acres, Sunshine, Gold Hill, Hidden Lake, and Altona can provide useful comparison records, but a driller still needs to evaluate your exact site.

sections.heading: What water yield can a Jamestown well provide?
sections.html:
Among wells with reported pump yields, the median is 6.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 5.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Most reported wells, 70%, fall in the 5-to-15-gallon-per-minute range. That is a workable result for many household systems when storage and the pump are designed correctly.

Results are not uniform. Twenty percent of wells report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, 7% report more than 15, and 3% report under 1. Only 676 wells report a pump yield, so the yield distribution does not describe every permitted well. Ask for a documented pump test, recovery information, and the intended household demand before treating a neighboring result as a guarantee.

sections.heading: What the water levels show near Jamestown
sections.html:
Only 79 wells report a static water level, so the water-level record is much thinner than the depth record. Where measurements exist, the median depth to water is 60 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 23 to 103 feet.

The decade medians suggest that measured water levels were generally deeper in the newer records: 21 feet in the 1960s, 25 feet in the 1970s, 50 feet in the 1980s, 49 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s. This pattern is a reason to investigate, not proof of a uniform regional decline. Different wells, locations, seasons, and measurement methods can affect the comparison. A buyer should obtain the actual well log and recent static and pumping levels for the property instead of relying only on the area median.

sections.heading: Jamestown drilling history and local permit records
sections.html:
Jamestown has a long record of domestic well development. The database contains 2,204 permitted wells, including 1,463 recorded as constructed and 1,487 with a reported total depth. The newest permit year in the records is 2025.

Permits were most numerous in the 1970s, with 517, followed by 385 in the 1990s, 366 in the 1980s, 192 in the 2000s, 112 in the 2010s, and 66 in the 2020s. The leading recorded drillers are Ground Water Systems Inc. (Wilson, Richard R.) with 513 wells, Ingram Drilling Inc. (Ingram, Stephen E.) with 214, and Walton with 185. These records show who has worked in the area; they are not a recommendation or a current availability list.

sections.heading: What does a new well cost near Jamestown?
sections.html:
Fractured mountain bedrock makes drilling cost sensitive to depth and ground conditions. The cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot. At the local median depth of 300 feet, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,500 to $30,000.

A finished system is more than the hole. With a pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work included, the estimated total at that median depth is $25,500 to $42,000. A shallow successful hole can cost less, while a deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grouting, and poor water production can change the bid. Get the drilling, testing, casing, pump, electrical, and site-work assumptions in writing. Also confirm whether the estimate includes a permit and any work needed to connect the well to the house.

sections.heading: Risks to check before building or buying in Jamestown
sections.html:
Most permits in this area are for domestic or household use, representing 94% of the use mix. The named aquifer records are dominated by unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers, with 2,123 wells, while 13 identify Fractured Crystalline and 8 identify Fractured Granite. There are no Denver Basin aquifer wells in the records. Fractured rock can produce a strong well, a marginal well, or a dry hole over short distances.

Water quality deserves its own investigation. Within about 10 miles, the mapped records include 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 610 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mappings do not establish contamination at your lot, but they support testing for site-appropriate contaminants. Before construction, confirm well separation from septic components, room for a replacement system, access for a drill rig, and the permit conditions for the planned use.

sections.heading: A practical plan for a Jamestown lot
sections.html:
Start with the property’s DWR permit, well construction report, pump test, static water level, and water-quality results. Then compare nearby records in Jamestown and areas such as Bark Ranch, Sunshine, Gold Hill, and Altona. The closest well is not always the best predictor in fractured bedrock, but a cluster of nearby logs can help a driller assess likely depth, casing, and water-bearing fractures.

For a new build, have the driller and excavation contractor review access before you buy. A mountain lot may need a workable route for a rig, room for spoils, and coordinated trenching, septic, electrical, and foundation work. Budget from the local $25,500-to-$42,000 finished-well estimate at median depth, then ask what happens if drilling goes deeper or production is low. Do not treat a permit alone as proof of a reliable household supply.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Jamestown, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Jamestown is 300 feet. The middle half runs from 160 to 480 feet, while the 90th-percentile depth is 620 feet. About 15% of recorded wells are 600 feet or deeper. Fractured granite, gneiss, access, and local fractures can make one lot differ sharply from another.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Jamestown?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 300-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $19,500 to $30,000. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $25,500 to $42,000. A bid can change with access, depth, casing, grouting, and water production.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Jamestown?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 6.0-gallon-per-minute median, with the middle half from 5.0 to 7.0 gallons per minute. Seventy percent of reported wells produce 5 to 15 gallons per minute, while 3% report under 1 gallon per minute. Only 676 wells report a yield, so confirm the property with a pump test.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Jamestown, Colorado?
faq.a: The records identify 14 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 610 historic mine features, and 58 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those locations do not prove contamination at a specific property. Test the well water for conditions relevant to the site, especially near mining or cleanup areas, and obtain recent laboratory results before buying.

faq.q: Are water levels dropping around Jamestown?
faq.a: The limited reported measurements show median depth to water of 21 feet in the 1960s, 25 feet in the 1970s, 50 feet in the 1980s, 49 feet in the 2010s, and 100 feet in the 2020s. Only 79 wells report static water levels, and the wells and conditions may differ. The pattern warrants property-specific review, not a definite conclusion of regional decline.
